title: The camera
content: A camera is an optical instrument that forms and records an image of an object.
e: A camera is an optical instrument that forms an image and records it on film or on an electronic sensor. A convex lens, a diaphragm, a shutter and a focusing ring share the work. Magnetic or thermal sensors are not what captures the picture.

title: Convex lens
content: A convex lens focuses the light from the object to form a real inverted image on the film or electronic sensor.
e: A camera uses a convex lens to converge light into a real inverted image on the film or sensor. A concave lens diverges and will not throw that real image onto the film. Cylindrical lenses are for astigmatism, not this focusing job.

title: Diaphragm
content: A diaphragm is placed behind the convex lens to control the amount of light energy falling on the film.
e: The diaphragm sits behind the convex lens and sets how much light energy reaches the film. It changes the aperture diameter. The shutter, not the diaphragm, sets how long the light is allowed in.

title: Aperture
content: The aperture is a circular opening through which the light passes. It can be made wide or narrow by adjusting the diaphragm. The size of the diameter of the aperture is expressed in term of f- numbers. The f- number of a camera is the ratio of the focal length of the lens to the diameter of aperture.
e: The aperture is the circular hole that light actually goes through. The diaphragm widens or narrows that hole, and the size is quoted as an f-number, focal length divided by diameter. A smaller f-number means a wider opening.

title: Shutter
content: A shutter controls the time during which light enters the camera through the lens.
e: The shutter times how long light may enter through the lens. That interval is the exposure time, which is how shutter speed is quoted. The diaphragm handles amount of light, not duration.

title: Focusing Ring
content: A camera consists of a focusing ring by which the distance between the lens and the film can be adjusted to obtain a sharp image on the film.
e: The focusing ring moves the lens toward or away from the film until the image is sharp. It is not a brightness control. Get the lens-to-film distance wrong and the picture stays blurred.

title: Film
content: The film at the back of the camera is actually a screen which receives the image. In a digital camera, the film is replaced by an electronic sensor. It is made up of millions of tiny pixels which response to light.
e: Film at the back of a camera is the screen that receives the image, with a thin silver-compound coating. A digital camera replaces that with a sensor of millions of pixels that respond to light. Gold chemistry is not what records the picture.

title: Human eye
content: Human eye consists of sense organs which are capable of receiving visual images and sending the information to the brain.
e: The eye receives a visual image and sends that information to the brain along the optic nerve. The brain then interprets the inverted retinal image as upright. Camera parts map onto cornea, iris, lens and retina in a similar division of labour.

title: Farsightedness (Hyperopia)
content: Farsightedness is a defect of vision in which distant objects are seen clearly, but objects nearby are blurry.
e: Farsightedness, hyperopia, means distant objects look sharp while nearby ones look blurry. Near rays meet behind the retina, so a converging convex spectacle lens adds the missing power. A diverging lens would make the near blur worse.

title: Nearsightedness (Myopia)
content: Nearsightedness is a defect of vision in which near objects are seen clearly, but objects far away are blurry.
e: Nearsightedness, myopia, means near objects look sharp while distant ones look blurry. Distant rays meet in front of the retina, so a diverging concave lens pushes the focus back. A converging lens would not correct that.

title: Least distance of distinct vision
content: People with normal vision can be seen an object in greatest detail when it is placed at a certain distance from the eye. This distance, which is known as the least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm.
e: The least distance of distinct vision is about 25 cm for a normal eye, the closest you can still see fine detail. Nearer than that, the eyelens cannot bulge enough. Infinity is the other end of the range, not this near point.

title: Maximum distance of distinct vision
content: People with normal vision can see clearly objects which are at infinity. Thus, for normal vision for the maximum distance of distinct vision is infinity.
e: For normal vision the far point is at infinity, so distant objects can be focused on the retina. That is the maximum distance of distinct vision. The near point, about 25 cm, is a different limit.

title: Compound microscope
content: A microscope is an optical instrument which uses lenses to make enlarged images of objects that are too small for the unaided eye to see.
e: A compound microscope uses at least two convex lenses to enlarge objects too small for the unaided eye. The objective throws a real magnified image, and the eyepiece magnifies that image again. Concave lenses will not build this instrument.

title: Electron microscope
content: Electron microscope is a microscope with high magnification and resolution, employing electron beams in place of light and using electron lenses.
e: An electron microscope replaces light with an electron beam and uses electron lenses. The much shorter electron wavelength gives higher magnification and resolution. Glass lenses for photons are not what focuses that beam.

title: Telescope
content: An optical instrument used for viewing distant objects is called a telescope.
e: A telescope is an optical instrument for viewing distant objects. A long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece work together. A microscope, by contrast, enlarges a nearby tiny object.

title: Astronomical telescope
content: The refracting astronomical telescope consists of an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length.
e: A refracting astronomical telescope uses an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length. The final image for a relaxed eye is virtual, inverted and magnified. Swapping those focal lengths would shrink the angular magnification.

title: Total reflecting prisms
content: Total reflecting prisms (90°, 45°, 45° prisms) are used in binoculars to reduce the length of the terrestrial telescope.
e: Right-angle 45-45-90 prisms in binoculars fold the path by total internal reflection. That shortens a terrestrial telescope and also erects the image. Ordinary glass plates without the critical-angle bounce will not do this folding.

title: Binocular
content: A binocular is an optical instrument which consists of a pair of telescopes one for each eye, and those telescope employ the total reflecting prism.
e: A binocular is a pair of telescopes, one for each eye, using total-reflecting prisms. You get a shortened, erect view with both eyes. A single shared telescope for both eyes is not a binocular.

title: Laser
content: A laser, acronym for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, is a source of a narrow beam of intense, monochromatic, coherent light in the visible, infrared or ultraviolet part of the electromagnetic radiation.
e: Laser stands for light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. The beam is narrow, intense, monochromatic and coherent. Spontaneous emission alone, or a jumble of random phases, is not a laser beam.

title: Spectrometer
content: A spectrometer is a scientific instrument used to separate and measure spectral components of a physical phenomenon.
e: A spectrometer separates and measures the spectral pieces of a physical signal. Wavelengths then fingerprint the source. A microscope magnifies shape; it does not by itself sort colour this way.

title: Photometry
content: Photometry is the science of measuring visible light in units that are weighted to the sensitive of human eye. The human eye responds only to light having wavelengths between about 400 nm and 700 nm.
e: Photometry measures visible light with weights that match the human eye. That eye responds from about 400 nm to 700 nm, not out to 900 nm. Luminous flux, intensity, luminance and illuminance are the main photometric quantities.

title: Luminance
content: Luminance L_v is the luminous intensity per unit area of light travelling in a given direction.
e: Luminance is luminous intensity per unit area of light travelling in a given direction. Its SI unit is candela per square metre. Lux is illuminance, the flux landing on a surface, not this outgoing quantity.

title: Inverse square law of illuminance
content: The luminance E_v at any point on the surface is inversely proportional to the square of the distance r between the source and the surface. This is known as inverse square law of illuminance.
e: Illuminance on a surface falls as the square of the distance from the source, times a cosine if the rays are oblique. Double the distance and the light on each square metre drops to one quarter. A direct proportion to r squared would be the wrong way round.
